People treat the class profile as if it were a report on us, and it is not. It is a recruiting document. It is written for the candidate who is sitting at a kitchen table trying to work out whether they belong here, and every number on it was chosen with that person in mind. Now, why the median and not the average. Because two or three people with very long careers pull the average up, and the moment it moves, everybody else on the page looks junior. The median does not move. It is the middle case, and the outliers sit on either side without touching it. And here is the thing I would most like candidates from smaller sectors to hear, because we say it publicly and almost nobody believes us. They look at four per cent and read it as a warning. It is the opposite. We are building a room, and a sector at four per cent is one we are short of.

I will tell you what I got wrong, because I spent about a month on it. I assumed everybody would be from finance or consulting, that their English would be better than mine, and that I would be the only person in the room who had never worked outside his own country. Three weeks in, none of that had survived contact with reality. Roughly a third of the room is not American. Several of them are considerably harder to understand than I am, and I say that with affection. And nobody cares. What I did not expect is what actually made me stand out. It was not the accent and it was certainly not my finance vocabulary. It was that I run a company I own, and that I have been in it for twenty-two years, which in that room is unusual. I spent the first month trying to sound like the people from finance, and it was a month I would like back.
